candidate.answerReason: Complementary consecutive blocks reduce the test to sums 6 and 7. Avoiding each sum forces one circular order up to rotation and reflection, and the two resulting orders are distinct.

methods.label: Use complementary blocks and force the neighbors
methods.explanation:
The total of the five numbers is \(15\). The complement of any nonempty proper consecutive block is also a consecutive block around the circle. Thus a sum \(s\) is available exactly when \(15-s\) is available.

Sums \(1\) through \(5\) are available as single numbers, so sums \(10\) through \(14\) are available as their complementary four-number blocks. The whole circle gives \(15\). Among the remaining sums, \(6\) pairs with \(9\), and \(7\) pairs with \(8\). Consequently an arrangement is bad exactly when it lacks sum \(6\) or sum \(7\).

To make \(6\), a two-number block must be \(\{1,5\}\) or \(\{2,4\}\). The only three-number set summing to \(6\) is \(\{1,2,3\}\); it is consecutive exactly when its complementary pair \(\{4,5\}\) is adjacent. A single number cannot give \(6\), and four numbers sum to at least \(10\). Therefore sum \(6\) is missing exactly when none of the pairs
\[
\{1,5\},\quad\{2,4\},\quad\{4,5\}
\]
is adjacent.

Under these restrictions, the two neighbors of \(4\) must be \(1\) and \(3\), while the two neighbors of \(5\) must be \(2\) and \(3\). This forces the chain \(1,4,3,5,2\), whose ends must join. Hence there is exactly one such circular order up to rotation and reflection:
\[
(1,4,3,5,2).
\]
The last and first entries are also neighbors. This order avoids all three forbidden pairs and therefore really does lack sum \(6\).

Similarly, sum \(7\) can come from the pairs \(\{2,5\}\), \(\{3,4\}\), or the triple \(\{1,2,4\}\). The triple is consecutive exactly when its complement \(\{3,5\}\) is adjacent. Thus missing \(7\) means avoiding the pairs
\[
\{2,5\},\quad\{3,4\},\quad\{3,5\}.
\]
Now \(3\) must have neighbors \(1\) and \(2\), and \(5\) must have neighbors \(1\) and \(4\). These force the chain \(2,3,1,5,4\), again leaving only one circular order up to rotation and reflection:
\[
(1,3,2,4,5).
\]
It avoids all three forbidden pairs, so it really does lack sum \(7\).

The first order has sum \(7\) from its adjacent \(3\) and \(4\), while the second lacks \(7\); hence the orders cannot be equivalent under rotation or reflection. Every bad arrangement belongs to one of the two cases, and each case gives exactly one class. The answer is \(\boxed{2}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
